title: Psalm 106: We Have Sinned Like Our Fathers
summary: After a call to praise and a personal prayer, the people confess that they have sinned like their ancestors. The psalm then retells Israel's history as a record of rebellion: at the Red Sea, in the wilderness cravings, in envy of Moses and Aaron, with the golden calf, in refusing the land, at Baal of Peor, at Meribah, and in Canaan, where they adopted the nations' idols and sacrificed their own children. Again and again God handed them over and then rescued them, remembering his covenant. The psalm ends with a plea to be gathered from the nations and a doxology that closes Book IV of the Psalter.
story: Psalm 106 is the second half of a pair with Psalm 105. Psalm 105 told the story from the exodus to the land as the record of God's faithfulness, without a word about Israel's failures. Psalm 106 tells much of the same story as a confession of Israel's unfaithfulness, carrying it on past the conquest into the period of the judges and beyond, all the way to exile among the nations. Together they give the whole truth: God kept his promises, and his people broke theirs. As the last psalm of Book IV, it brings that book's reflection on the loss of the kingdom to a close with honest confession and a prayer for return, and its final verse is the doxology that marks the end of the collection.
historical:
The psalm has no heading beyond the opening Hallelujah, and verse 47, “gather us from the nations”, strongly suggests it was prayed by Israelites scattered in exile, after the Babylonian conquest of Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC, or by a community back in the land still waiting for the rest of its people to return. Verses 1 and 47 to 48 appear in 1 Chronicles 16:34-36, at the end of the song sung when the ark came to Jerusalem; as with Psalms 96 and 105, scholars debate which text came first. Many think verse 48, “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting”, was added as the formal close of Book IV, matching the doxologies at the end of Books I to III (Psalms 41:13; 72:18-19; 89:52).

The episodes follow the Torah and the history books: the rebellion at the Red Sea (Exodus 14), the craving for meat (Numbers 11), the revolt of Dathan and Abiram (Numbers 16), the golden calf at Horeb, another name for Sinai (Exodus 32), the refusal to enter the land (Numbers 13 and 14), the worship of Baal of Peor and the zeal of Phinehas (Numbers 25), the waters of Meribah (Numbers 20), and the idolatry of the judges and kings (Judges 2; 2 Kings 17 and 21).
cultural:
Communal confession was a recognized form of prayer in Israel, especially after the exile. Ezra 9, Nehemiah 9, and Daniel 9 all contain long prayers in which the people confess not only their own sins but their ancestors', and trace the nation's history as a story of rebellion met by mercy. Psalm 106 belongs to that tradition. To say “We have sinned like our fathers” (verse 6) was to refuse to blame the previous generation alone.

The sins named are those Israel's neighbors would have seen as ordinary religion. Baal of Peor was a local form of the Canaanite god Baal worshiped in Moab, and eating sacrifices offered to the dead or to lifeless gods (verse 28) was part of that worship. Child sacrifice, which the Torah forbids (Leviticus 18:21; Deuteronomy 12:31), was practiced in the region and is recorded among Israel's kings (2 Kings 16:3; 21:6). The psalm calls the gods who received such offerings “demons” (verse 37), a rare word that treats them as real but malign powers rather than true gods. The image of Moses standing “in the breach” (verse 23) comes from warfare: a soldier filling a gap in a broken city wall to stop the enemy pouring through.
literary: The psalm is framed by praise (verses 1 to 5) and petition (verses 47 and 48). Verse 6 states the confession that governs the rest, and the history that follows is arranged as a series of episodes, each with a similar rhythm: God acted, the people forgot or rebelled, God judged, and someone intervened or God relented. Moses (verse 23) and Phinehas (verse 30) stand in the gap. The word “remember” marks the turns: the fathers did not remember God's kindness (verse 7), the psalmist asks God to remember him (verse 4), and at the end God remembered his covenant (verse 45). Verses 40 to 46 summarize the whole cycle of judgment and mercy, the same pattern the book of Judges describes, and the plea of verse 47 asks God to repeat it once more.

outline.t: Praise, and a prayer to share in God's favor
We have sinned: rebellion and rescue at the Red Sea
Craving and envy in the wilderness
The golden calf and Moses in the breach
Refusing the land, Baal of Peor, and Meribah
Idolatry in Canaan, judgment, and repeated mercy
Gather us from the nations; the doxology closing Book IV

doctrines.note: The psalm models corporate confession. The people do not excuse themselves by blaming their ancestors; they place themselves in the same line: “We have sinned like our fathers”. Honest repentance tells the whole story, including one's own part.

Idolatry is pictured as an exchange: they traded “their Glory for the image of a grass-eating ox”. The psalm traces how it led from worship to child sacrifice, showing that false worship reshapes a whole society.

God's faithfulness outlasts Israel's unfaithfulness. Despite repeated rebellion, “He remembered His covenant with them, and relented by the abundance of His loving devotion”. The covenant holds because of God, not because of Israel.

words.note: Perets, a breach or gap, especially in a wall. Moses stood “in the breach” between God's wrath and the people. Ezekiel 22:30 uses the same picture when God looks for someone to stand in the gap and finds no one.

Chashav, to count, reckon, or credit. Phinehas's act “was credited to him as righteousness” (verse 31), language that echoes Genesis 15:6, where Abraham's faith was credited to him as righteousness. Paul builds his argument in Romans 4 on the Genesis text.
Mur, to exchange or trade. The people exchanged their Glory, the living God, for the image of an ox. The word frames idolatry as a bad trade, giving up what is priceless for what is worthless.

Nacham, to relent, be sorry, or change course. When used of God it describes his turning from announced judgment in response to intercession or repentance (Exodus 32:14). Verse 45 grounds that turning in his abundant loving devotion.

christ: Paul's description of humanity exchanging the glory of the immortal God for images resembling animals (Romans 1:23) echoes verse 20 of this psalm, applying Israel's golden-calf sin to the whole human race. The psalm's intercessors, Moses standing in the breach and Phinehas turning away the plague, point toward the New Testament's picture of Christ as the one mediator between God and humanity (1 Timothy 2:5), who does not merely stand in the gap but bears the judgment himself. And the prayer “gather us from the nations” finds an answer in the gospel's gathering of scattered people, Jew and Gentile, into one people of God (John 11:52). The link is thematic: the psalm's cycle of rebellion and mercy is the story the gospel claims to break open.

hard.q: The psalm faults Israel for not destroying the peoples of Canaan and praises Phinehas for a killing. How should a reader take this?
hard.a: Verse 34 refers to the command in Deuteronomy 7 and 20 to destroy the nations of Canaan, one of the hardest parts of the Old Testament for modern readers, and verse 30 recalls Phinehas killing an Israelite man and a Midianite woman during the plague at Peor (Numbers 25:6-8). The psalm's concern is religious rather than ethnic: the failure it condemns is that Israel “mingled with the nations and adopted their customs”, ending in idolatry and the sacrifice of children. Interpreters take the conquest texts in several ways. Some read them as a unique, limited act of judgment on specific societies, not a pattern for later generations; others point to hyperbolic war language common in ancient Near Eastern records; others stress that the Old Testament itself shows the Canaanite peoples surviving and being incorporated. Christians generally agree that these commands are not a license for violence today, since the New Testament directs the fight against idolatry to the heart and the church rather than to the sword.

questions: The psalmist says “We have sinned like our fathers” rather than blaming them. What would honest confession of your family's, church's, or nation's history look like?
The Israelites “soon forgot His works” right after singing his praise. What makes gratitude fade so quickly?
What might it mean for you to stand in the breach for someone else in prayer?
